author: Newsweek
title: Trump's Approval Rating Fluctuates With Iran Ceasefire Stability, Latest Remarks May Trigger New Decline
text:
President Trump's approval ratings have risen and fallen in direct correlation with the status of the Iran ceasefire throughout 2026, according to Nate Silver's data. After declaring the truce "over" following new attacks and U.S. strikes, a pattern suggests his numbers may soon drop again, while oil markets react to escalated tensions.
The political fortunes of President Donald Trump in 2026 have been tightly linked to the status of a ceasefire in the conflict with Iran, with his approval ratings rising and falling in near-perfect sync with the truce's stability since the war began in February.
Data aggregated by Nate Silver's Bulletin shows that every collapse of the ceasefire has dragged down Trump's numbers, while each period of calm has allowed them to recover. As of Wednesday, before the latest developments, his approval stood at 43.1 percent and disapproval at 52.7 percent, holding relatively steady since early July after a rocky stretch in late June when ceasefire violations pushed disapproval to 54.4 percent.
The pattern first emerged after the war's opening: Trump's approval hit a 2026 low of 41.6 percent on February 26, just days after joint U.S. and Israeli strikes killed Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and launched the conflict. That nadir followed a brief bump from the January 3 capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro. The first significant rebound came in April after Trump extended the ceasefire indefinitely on April 20, lifting approval to 44.4 percent, its peak for the year.
A May 24 report of a nearing broader peace agreement pushed approval to 43.3 percent, but an Iranian attack on the UAE on May 4, coinciding with Trump's announcement of "Project Freedom" to protect shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, sent approval tumbling to 41.9 percent by May 12. The June 17 memorandum of understanding between Trump and Iranian officials then stabilized ratings, setting the stage for the July plateau.
On Wednesday, speaking at the NATO summit in Ankara, Turkey, Trump declared the ceasefire "over" following Iranian attacks on commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz and U.S. retaliatory strikes, saying "As far as I'm concerned it's just a waste of time.
" Hours later, the U.S. launched another round of strikes on Iran, effectively terminating the truce. His remarks and the renewed strikes sparked fears of a wider war and sent oil prices surging due to concerns about disruption to the vital Strait of Hormuz energy shipments. Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi countered on social media that Trump's comments "are not a sign of power but an admission of the failure" of U.S. policy.
Trump's statement also highlighted internal Iranian divisions: hard-liners seek to maintain control over the waterway as leverage, while pragmatists favor a lasting peace to lift sanctions and revive the economy. Formal negotiations, scheduled after the funeral of Supreme Leader Khamenei (which ended Thursday), are expected to address the Strait's full reopening and Iran's nuclear program.
While Trump proclaimed the ceasefire ended, he did not rule out talks, referring to his envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and noting "but they have to come back to me.
" The Silver Bulletin average had not yet captured public reaction to these Ankara comments at the time of reporting
